rv.q: An exuberant, inventive "The Wiz Live!" on Thursday night breathed new life into the notion of full-scale musicals on live TV with a happy serving of 70s soul and R&B;, updated with a 2015 vibe.
This revival of 'The Wiz' brings fresh energy and spectacular design to the beloved musical, though it occasionally feels overstuffed with contemporary references that don't always land.

The cast has some other familiar faces, including no less than Deborah Cox as Glinda, an L. Frank Baum character that might have morphed into the star of “Wicked,” but who was woefully underwritten in “The Wiz.”
In this second major Broadway revival, the show’s extravagant display of Black magical realism and its persistent humor blaze over the technical challenges.
'The Wiz' is a pleasant, serviceable time at the theater
The effect was, as with so much of the revival, of missing out on a moment that could have been great, if only given more care and fine tuning.
The new Broadway revival is charming, but at the cost of a broader artistic vision
Dizzying visuals and overamplification too often swallow both actors and storytelling in a swirling sensory overload.
Despite the cozy feeling of being reunited with beloved material 40 years after it was last on Broadway, director Schele Williams’ production is deflatingly flimsy and lackluster.
The road to success might have a few bricks missing, but it’s a golden one nonetheless.

In other words, the actors and dancers in this “Wiz” carry the show magnificently, with Kyle Ramar Freeman’s Lion, Phillip Johnson Richardson’s Tin Man and Avery Wilson’s Scarecrow the funniest trio of misfits ever to take us on this trip to Oz.
They may still ease on down the (non yellow brick) road, but there’s little sense of ease.
Then again, if you’re just up for a good time, you can ease on down here in comfort and confidence.
Charlie Smalls' score is packed with infectious grooves and the cast delivers some fine singing.

But this Wiz mounts in appeal and becomes so alternately giddy and moving that after a while I forgot to be annoyed by the “Believe in yourself” homilies and the endless succession of overripe set projections.
A smarter, warmer, bolder revival of The Wiz remains tantalizingly out of reach, but Lewis delivers brains, heart, and courage all on her own.
It can't be denied that the musical is flawed.
This production, which is the equivalent of a disco-themed karaoke party, just makes me feel disappointed.
What’s on view right now isn’t even “fine” for 2024.
This is as lifeless a production as I’ve ever seen on Broadway, and, quite frankly, it’s shocking.
Tonight NBC proved my faith was well placed with a musical event that was finally worth watching and not just hate-watching.

Dorothy’s back on Broadway in a reimagined revival of The Wiz. Does the fresh take with new material by Amber Ruffin and movement by Beyonce’s “Single Ladies” choreographer JaQuel Knight ease on down the road? For the most part, with a few stumbles along the way.
With an energetic cast, splashy and highly colorful design, and a collection of pleasant and enjoyable songs, The Wiz is still a diverting musical comedy.
They played into it to expose it and celebrate that we’ve come far enough that White theatregoers like me were attuned to the discomfort.

Still Broadway audiences deserve something far better than this middling national-tour production that has been dropped into the Marquis for a limited run the same way Dorothy’s house was dropped into Oz after a tornado.
